canberra.title: Labor ministers contradicting each other over ATO credit card ban
canberra.snippet: Federal Labor ministers can’t seem to agree on the tax office’s decision to ban credit card payments, inviting ridicule from the Coalitio...
canberra.content:
Housing Minister Clare O’Neil says the government has ‘real concerns’ over the ATO’s decision to ban credit card payments. Photo: Facebook.

Federal Labor ministers can’t seem to agree on the tax office’s decision to ban credit card payments, inviting ridicule from the Coalition and adding uncertainty for small businesses.

After the government’s card payment surcharge ban took effect this month, the Australian Taxation Office announced it would no longer accept credit card payments after 30 November because it could not absorb the fees.

That decision caused an immediate backlash from the business sector, which has to absorb the fees.

It accused the ATO of hypocrisy and pointed out that many small businesses pay their taxes via credit card to manage their cash flow.

After crisis meetings with business groups this week, the ATO remains steadfast in its decision.

On Thursday morning (8 October), however, Housing Minister Clare O’Neil told Channel Nine the government had “real concerns” over the ATO’s decision.

“We really want the ATO to go back and talk to business about what they’ve decided to do here, and think about how they can find a solution that works,” she said.

The minister defended the surcharge ban, which came about after a Reserve Bank review of the payments, but suggested the ATO should not have banned credit card payments.

This followed Small Business Minister Anne Aly (through another media interview the day before) calling on the ATO to reverse its ban on credit card payments, saying there had been no consultation over the move.

She urged the ATO to keep talking with the business sector to find a “way forward”.

But Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton told ABC’s Radio National that Labor was happy with the tax office’s move.

“The government supports the ATO’s decision,” he said.

“The ATO has made that decision because of the principle of consistency between the private sector and the public sector … and that is that if we’re saying that surcharges can’t exist in the private sector, then surcharges shouldn’t exist in the public sector.”

The assistant minister even went so far as to say he didn’t see why businesses would have to increase prices to absorb credit card fees because processing fees had fallen.

“That reduction means that card payments are cheaper for businesses to process,” Dr Charlron said.

“So there’s no reason, as a result of this reform, that consumers should be paying more when they tap their card for a coffee.

“The cost to the business has gone down. There’s no reason why that should be greater than what they were paying before in terms of the price and the surcharge.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says that all means the government doesn’t know where it stands in relation to the ATO’s decision.

“We have seen Labor in the last 24 hours all over the shop when it comes to small businesses being able to use credit cards with the ATO. All over the shop,” Mr Taylor said.

“We’ve had the Housing Minister in one place, the Small Business Minister somewhere else, and the de facto Treasurer has been defending the ATO.

“In fact, what I hear from Labor is more willingness to defend the tax office than to defend small business. Well, that’s not surprising, because so few of them have worked in small business.

“But they should, from today, get rid of the ban, axe the ban that they’ve put on the ability of small businesses to pay tax with their credit cards.

“They [the government] don’t want to pay the surcharge, and yet, in the last couple of days, they’ve said to small businesses ‘you’ve got to absorb the surcharges’.

“The hypocrisy of this government knows no bounds, because they don’t understand enterprise. They don’t understand the hard work of small business people who are the backbone of this nation.”

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson laughed at the government’s expense, saying the disagreement between ministers was merely jostling for Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ job.

“I think what we are seeing is an audition for who his replacement is going to be between Clare O’Neil and Andrew Charlton over this,” Mr Wilson told News24.

“One of the problems we have is an inconsistency where the government is turning around to small businesses and is saying you’ve got to cop the extra costs that are being passed on by the banks, but we, the government, won’t.”

canberra.title: Public school budget claims rejected but parents urge government to be more up front on funding changes
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has pushed back against media reports claiming school budget cuts will leave schools in poorer areas worse off, saying...
canberra.content:
Public school budgets are changing, but by how much is still to be decided. Photo: ACT Public Schools.

The ACT Government has pushed back against media reports claiming school budget cuts will leave schools in poorer areas worse off, saying the data was incomplete and did not include all funding sources.

But school communities remain concerned about the funding process and what it will mean for their students and families next year.

One media outlet used leaked school budget figures to show that less well-off schools such as Kingsford Smith, Caroline Chisholm and Theodore Primary would take cuts while wealthy schools such as Garran, Hughes and Aranda would be better off.

It said that in 2027 Kingsford Smith would incur almost a 25 per cent cut amounting to $3.5 million, while Caroline Chisholm would lose $1.5 million and Theodore $300,000 or 8 per cent.

But Garran, Hughes and Aranda budgets would be boosted by 7.8 per cent, 5.6 per cent and 4.2 per cent respectively.

If true, this would defeat the purpose of the government’s funding revamp, which is designed to bring school budgets under control and build a fairer, needs-based system.

A government spokesperson said some of the published figures were incomplete and did not include all available sources of funding such as additional specialist-school funding and complex-behaviour support funding.

School principals were given indicative 2027 budgets based on their Student Resource Allocation, but these were starting points.

“No ACT public school has had its budget finalised for 2027, and no final decisions have been made about staffing profiles or individual employees,” the spokesperson said.

“The directorate will continue to work with and support schools throughout the process, recognising that no two schools are the same.”

Final 2027 school staffing profiles will be provided to schools in week 5 of Term 4.

The spokesperson said 2027 funding decisions were being made using a consistent, needs-based approach, with a clear focus on equity, student outcomes and the long-term sustainability of the public education system.

This aligns with the recommendations of the Public School System Resourcing Review, which found early childhood and primary schools faced higher cost pressures and identified opportunities to improve fairness and consistency in how funding was allocated, including moving to a centralised system.

“This is an important step towards returning to a more equitable system,” the spokesperson said.

“Adjustments are made to school budget allocations to account for students with disability, complex student needs and behaviours, and occupational violence risk.”

ACT Parents executive officer Veronica Elliott says schools need time to adjust. Photo: ACT Parents.

But the Public School System Resourcing Review also found the SRA was flawed and recommended a full review.

In the meantime, targeted changes have been made for 2027 to improve equity and strengthen needs-based funding, including implementing the Adjustments-Based Resourcing Model, increasing direct support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, maintaining funding for specialist schools and redistributing some college funding to schools in need.

But even with adjustments and top-ups, schools and parents remain worried about where budgets will land.

ACT Parents executive officer Veronica Elliott said her members wanted more transparency and communication from the government around funding, and a more staged approach to the associated move to the centralised single system.

“What we can see from the Public School Resourcing Review is that there are opportunities to increase the efficiency of the public school system by adopting the one public education system and creating a more centralised approach that delivers consistency to schools, will naturally provide efficiencies of scale, and that could be something that delivers some relief on school budgets,” she said.

But Ms Elliott said the SRA should have been reviewed first and then structures put in place to support schools through the changes.

“We’d like to see a staged approach to the changes that we’re asking schools to make, so that these can be undertaken in a strategic and considered way, rather than implementing a budget decision that requires schools to do the work, where the system doesn’t have the supports available or the guidance already available for them to follow,” she said.

“I’m concerned that we’re asking schools to make changes to how they operate next year without having any formalised guidance on what we’re asking them to do.”

Ms Elliott doubted whether the SRA review would even be completed for the 2028 school year.

The government spokespersons said the 2026-27 ACT Budget allocated $1.2 billion to public schools, a 7.3 per cent increase on the 2025-26 Budget.

A total of $40.58 million went to support 2027 school budgets as the system worked to bring its collective overspend back within its approved funding envelope.

“Additional investment does not remove the need for careful stewardship of public resources,” the spokesperson said.

“The Directorate has a responsibility to ensure funding is used in a way that maximises benefits for students and supports high-quality teaching and learning.”

The Public School System Resourcing Review was prompted by budget overruns in 77 of 92 schools during 2025, and assessed how to allocate resources more equitably and sustainably.

canberra.title: Alleged killer driver charged with manslaughter over Bega hit-and-run
canberra.snippet: A police manhunt for the driver accused of killing an elderly man in a road rage incident has resulted in a woman’s arrest this wee...
canberra.content:
8 October 2026

Trevor Fleet (right) was allegedly killed after he was hit by a car in Bega. Photo: NSW Police.

A police manhunt for the driver accused of killing an elderly man in a road rage incident has resulted in a woman’s arrest this week.

Trevor Fleet, a 73-year-old from Eden, was driving in Bega with his partner around midday on 31 August 2026 when he had an interaction with the female driver of another car.

Police allege the pair both stopped on Newtown Road, near the intersection with the Princes Highway, then got out and spoke to each other face-to-face.

It is alleged the woman got back into her vehicle and reversed, hitting Mr Fleet, before driving away.

Paramedics treated him at the scene before he was taken to hospital in a serious condition. He died from his injuries on 1 September.

Last month, police launched a public appeal in an attempt to find his alleged killer.

Then on Wednesday (7 October), police raided a home in the Bega Valley town of Wyndham as well as a business in South Pambula.

“During the searches, police seized a silver Holden SUV believed to be associated with the investigation, along with a number of other items that will undergo further forensic examination,” a NSW Police spokesperson said.

In addition, police arrested 41-year-old Melinda Jane Avison and charged her with manslaughter.

The pink-haired woman needed to be physically supported when she was escorted into a cell by Corrective Services officers to face the NSW Local Court over an audio-visual link on Thursday (8 October)

Her lawyer, Rosemary Benet, said her client was unwell when she spoke to her, and she would not be applying for bail.

In addition to needing medication for her mental health conditions, Ms Benet said her client had a broken toe.

Judge Te’res Sia formally refused Ms Avison bail and remanded her in custody to next face the Bega Local Court over an audio-visual link on 15 December. No plea was entered.

canberra.title: UC casuals win 17% super under new pay deal
canberra.snippet: Casual academic staff at the University of Canberra are big winners under a new pay deal that boosts superannuation contributions to 17 p...
canberra.content:
University of Canberra staff have backed a new Enterprise Agreement. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Casual academic staff at the University of Canberra are big winners under a new pay deal that boosts superannuation contributions to 17 per cent by 2030.

UC staff have voted in favour of the proposed University’s Enterprise Agreement 2026, that will also ensure casual staff continue to have access to benefits including up to 30 weeks’ paid parental leave for primary carers, long service leave and expanded opportunities for professional and career development.

Current and former casual staff have also begun being reimbursed for historic underpayments over six years.

Under the new pay deal, staff will receive a total salary increase of 14.5 per cent across five pay rises, equating to about 15.35 per cent when compounded.

The new Agreement also includes new wellbeing, flexibility and leave provisions; stronger workload and consultation processes; expanded support for Indigenous staff; improved parental leave arrangements; and measures supporting the responsible use of artificial intelligence in the workplace.

UC said the increased benefits for casual staff would help build greater long-term financial security for an important cohort of the University’s workforce.

Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten said the move to 17 per cent superannuation for casual staff was a significant investment in staff and recognised the important contribution casual employees made to the University community.

“It provides greater retirement savings and financial security, and ensures casual staff have access to some of the most competitive employment benefits in the sector,” he said.

Professor Shorten said the new Enterprise Agreement was good for staff and provided confidence for the years ahead.

“This is a positive outcome for our staff and the University,” he said. “This Enterprise Agreement rewards our people, strengthens our employment framework and supports the University’s future.”

Mr Shorten said the University remained committed to fostering a workplace that recognised and rewarded its people while supporting the flexibility, wellbeing and opportunities they needed to thrive.

“This Enterprise Agreement provides a strong foundation as we continue to deliver for our students, staff and the Canberra community,” he said.

UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten has apologised for underpaying casual staff. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The University will now submit the Enterprise Agreement to the Fair Work Commission for approval. It will come into effect 21 days after approval.

UC has also resolved the underpayment of casuals over a six-year period, reimbursing 255 current and former staff with more than $240,000.

UC launched a review of payments to casual academic staff in October last year, covering July 2019 to December 2025.

The total value of identified underpayments amounted to $243,979.95, excluding superannuation and interest.

The University has started contacting those affected, and current casual staff began receiving payments from Tuesday (6 October).

It said the underpayments arose where PhD qualifications were not recognised in payment rates, Unit Convenor responsibilities were not reflected in payment rates and lecture and tutorial payments were incorrectly classified as repeat rather than initial rates.

A separate review of casual academic marking practices was underway to determine whether staff have been appropriately paid for marking activities.

Professor Shorten apologised to the current and former casual academic staff who were underpaid.

“It is disappointing. I deeply regret that these historic errors occurred. On behalf of the University, I sincerely apologise to everyone who has been affected,” he said.

“The University has taken the process very seriously, and our checks have been thorough. We are committed to making sure that every affected staff member receives the money they are owed as soon as possible.”

The University has also moved to improve record-keeping and governance arrangements to prevent further errors.

Professor Shorten said transparency and accountability would remain central.

“We have self-reported these findings to the Fair Work Ombudsman and continue to work constructively with the Ombudsman throughout this process,” he said.

“My focus is on supporting affected staff, addressing identified issues and building stronger systems that give our people confidence that they are being paid 100 per cent correctly.”

The University said it had verified and paid casual staff payments made since January 2026 correctly.

australia.title: In an overgrown ‘swamp’ in Rookwood cemetery, Jayne asks: ‘Where are the graves? She’s told: ‘You’re standing on them’
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Years-long search for family ends in shock, fury – and a 16-year quest to stop NSW Health burying people in unmarked graves Fi...
australia.content:
Jayne Kinsolving remembers wading through knee-high shrubs to find her family’s grave.

The feeling of vines and thorns tearing at her legs. The squelch of her footsteps across water-logged soil.

Jayne and her foster mother, Barbara Davis, had arrived at this strange corner of Sydney’s Rookwood cemetery 16 years ago to see the place where Jayne’s biological mother, Christine Halpin, her sister Jessica and grandmother Patricia were buried.

The cemetery had assigned a staff member to guide them to the spot.

A piece of paper with a handwritten guide to the grave’s location described it as being in section “NNNN”. The plot number was left blank.

Jayne and Barbara remember stopping at a large depression in the earth. Metal stakes had been driven into the ground, just visible above the overgrown grass.

Jayne describes it as a swamp. “It was disgusting,” she says.

She remembers turning to their guide. “I was like, ‘Where are the graves?’ And he looked at me and he said, ‘You’re standing on them.’

“We had been walking on grave after grave after grave. And Mum and I started to cry and we stepped to the side.”

Jayne had been searching for her family for years. Christine was 18 when Jayne was born. Unable to look after her baby, Christine had turned to Barbara – her own beloved foster mother – to care for the newborn.

Jayne’s search ended when researchers at the Salvation Army told her that Christine had died in a house fire in 1989, a month before her eighth birthday.

The state government had deemed the family too poor to afford their own funeral. They were buried in an unmarked communal grave at Rookwood.

The visit sparked in Barbara fury and a steely determination.

She had cared deeply for Christine, having acted as her foster carer for four years. No one told her that Christine would be placed in a grave of this kind, or asked whether she would fund a proper burial.

The plain-talking shop owner from Lake Macquarie, a stalwart of the local business sector and a former member of the Newcastle Knights board, got to work.

She lobbied the government, wrote submissions to parliament and went to the press, eventually securing a commitment in 2013 from the then Liberal government that all graves would be marked.

“I did kick up about that because I thought they deserved to have a better resting place than that,” Barbara says.

“We’re not that poor a nation, we can throw our money overseas and give it away … but we can’t look after our own.

“How much would it have cost to put a cross with their names on it? Why couldn’t that have gone up?”

A Guardian Australia investigation has revealed that, despite the pledge to Barbara, the use of unmarked communal graves has continued in large numbers, albeit in different sections of Rookwood.

Using evidence from friends and family, analysis of cemetery registries and satellite imagery, the investigation has identified hundreds of unmarked graves, often containing the remains of four to six people. The burials are taking place in stretches of the cemetery that are better cared for than the “swamp” Jayne and Barbara visited.

But the vast majority are completely unmarked. Only about a dozen have markings of any kind. A 17-metre stretch of graves dug for burials conducted in 2026, estimated to contain the remains of more than 40 people, does not have a single marker.

“It is a disgrace,” Barbara says. “Whether you’re a prince or a pauper, you deserve a decent burial site, even just with a wooden cross with your name on it.”

Asked about the state government’s 2013 promise to begin marking graves, the operator of Rookwood said: “Metropolitan Memorial Parks has not identified a legislative or regulatory requirement giving effect to that statement.”

The operator said the government had not funded it to provide grave markings.

The Guardian’s investigation prompted an apology from NSW Health, which has flagged changes to improve the process.

The NSW health minister, Ryan Park, described the failings as “unacceptable”, and on Tuesday said his department would explore reforms, including emulating the Victorian model, where individuals are buried with their own plot and marking.

“I think it’s something that we need to do better,” Park said. “Quite clearly, the dignity of those who have … passed, as well as for their families, is something that we need to take into consideration, and we need to do this better.”

The Guardian has also found multiple cases in which the state government has not properly notified friends, family or those associated with the deceased, to give them the chance to intervene and pay for a proper funeral.

“That’s all anyone really asks for,” Jayne says. “If we had had that opportunity, then they wouldn’t be in a pauper’s grave that was left in that condition.

“That’s all any family or any of their loved ones wants a chance to do.”

Homelessness support services also say they are not being notified before their clients are put into the graves, despite the NSW health department’s own policy document suggesting authorities check with organisations associated with the deceased while they were alive.

In place of the site visited by Jayne and Barbara, the cemetery operator has placed a path of remembrance, opened in 2017. It is used to offer members of the public the chance to pay $880 for a plaque on a rock to commemorate people in unmarked graves.

There are only about a few dozen plaques for deaths after 2020. There have been hundreds of burials and ash internments in that period.

Many of the other plaques honour babies who were stillborn or commemorate historic deaths in the mid- to late-1900s.

There is no plaque for the Halpins, despite Barbara’s campaigning.

“It’s almost just like they did enough to shut people up,” Jayne says. “That’s honestly how it feels.

“They would not want that for themselves or those in their families. But it’s looking and sounding like they did the bare minimum – or just enough to get Mum off their case.”

australia.title: One Nation’s AI video is vile and tired – but the ensloppification of Australian politics doesn’t stop there
australia.snippet: The inflammatory clip shows the wild west of online politicking created by unrestricted access to AI – and why watchdogs need more powers...
australia.content:
One Nation’s new AI-generated campaign video is a new low – even for them.

The video – reportedly played at the party’s Victorian campaign launch over the weekend – is an AI-generated collection of racist tropes, depicting a man who appears to be African brandishing a machete, an apparently Middle Eastern man with an explosive vest, a South Asian man in a turban talking about “mass migration” and an Indigenous elder talking about people receiving “money … on the basis of need, not identity”.

But the inflammatory clip says more about the wild west of online politicking created by cheap, unrestricted access to AI videos, and why governments need to empower watchdog bodies to do more about it.

The video was barely mentioned in most media reporting, which otherwise largely focused on the rousing reception Pauline Hanson received from her supporters, the music that was played over loudspeakers and the Trump-esque pledge from candidate Mark Nicholson – the producer of the “Please Explain” cartoon series – to jail Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan. Guardian Australia, previously barred from One Nation events, did not attempt to attend Saturday’s launch.

Coverage has focused on the first part of the video, an AI-generated scene of a young man “coming out” as a conservative to his leftwing family. As progressive campaign group GetUp observed, it’s a scene cribbing from a similar Israeli campaign video from Benjamin Netanyahu.

It could also be pointed out how tired the gags are. Blue-haired hipsters with nose rings, eating mung beans? Revolutionary. Were the jokes generated by ChatGPT as well?

There’s an argument for ignoring it entirely, so as to not give it the attention and free advertising the party obviously wants. It is rage bait, seeking to draw a response and then complain about the response as further proof that One Nation is being “picked on” or is “riling up the lefties”. The response of a Hobart cafe frequented by Hanson’s daughter Lee pledging to donate takings from One Nation customers to the Greens – and accompanied by predictable “genuine hurt” from the younger Hanson – was entirely on script.

But for all the bad taste, there’s little anyone can do about it right now.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority cannot take action, because its powers don’t extend to this kind of content, and the video thus far seems to only exist online – not promoted in broadcast forms. Electoral commissions only have powers to regulate misinformation about the electoral process – not lies or distasteful content.

The federal Labor government has so far shrugged off growing calls from inside and outside parliament to ban the use of AI-generated content in election periods. As the government works to legislate around a raft of AI-related harms this year, the time would be ripe to deal with this long-ignored issue.

News Corp reported a One Nation spokesperson saying they were preparing “another version for broadcast”. That could technically put it inside Acma’s remit, but the tone of the ad is unlikely to breach current broadcasting rules, one industry source said.

So, then, is there something to the idea of clamping down on AI-generated content more broadly? Senator David Pocock thinks so: he’s been pushing for two years for the government to address generative AI around election campaigns, with 35,000 people signing his online petition calling for Labor to “legislate a ban on the use of deepfakes in elections before the next federal election”.

This week, the parliament’s joint committee on AI heard from witnesses saying action was overdue. The AEC said in a submission to the inquiry that AI makes it “more difficult for people to distinguish between authentic and manipulated content, increase[s] confusion about authoritative sources of information, and create[s] challenges for [electoral agencies]”.

“Inauthentic content or deepfakes circulating during the voting period, for instance, may well compromise the actual or perceived integrity of an election.”

These are not new concerns. A parliamentary report from October 2024 warned of AI “being used to adversely influence or undermine electoral and democratic processes” and “to deceive the public, create or exacerbate bias or influence public opinion or sentiment corrosively”.

Of course, the One Nation video is a different beast. No voter is being tricked into thinking a leftwing family has really changed its allegiances. But it should open the door to a wider discussion about whether this kind of content is appropriate for an election campaign.

AI lowers the barrier for entry for making such inflammatory videos. Normally, it would be harder – and more expensive – to hire a film crew and actors willing to act out such rhetoric.

In 2024, the Macquarie Dictionary named “enshittification” as its word of the year, defining the term as: “The gradual deterioration of a service or product brought about by a reduction in the quality of service provided, especially of an online platform, and as a consequence of profit-seeking.” Even casual users of Facebook, X, email platforms, Google search and basically any online marketplace would be familiar with the term.

Australian politics, like many parts of the world economy, is enduring what I’m calling “ensloppification”: the permeation of AI-generated slop into every crevice of society – and politics is not immune.

This week we have seen conservative campaign group Advance’s own Victorian AI ad, picturing a Labor election win as Daniel Andrews pops champagne corks and leads a conga line. Liberal MP Jason Wood was factchecked by AAP for posting “a fake image of Anthony Albanese arriving at a deserted airport”, while AAP has also debunked numerous AI-generated political interview-style videos purportedly shot outside Parliament House.

Prof Terry Flew, of the Centre for AI Trust and Governance, told the inquiry on Wednesday that Australia had no single agency to address all misinformation risks, but recommended that government consider prohibiting AI-generated deepfakes during election periods.

“There are real risks that AI-generated misinformation, as well as what has come to be known as ‘AI slop’, will further erode public trust in institutions and degrade the wider information ecosystem,” Flew said.

“[AI-generated deepfakes go] beyond the legitimate bounds of public campaigning and prove to be genuinely threatening to the individuals and groups who are the targets of them.”

  • Josh Butler is a Guardian Australia political reporter and chief of staff in Canberra

australia.title: From dashing romantic reality star to DV charges: how it all went wrong for Bachelor Sam Wood
australia.snippet: Wood’s cultural prominence, commercial success and now collapse of his empire was shaped by the confected TV narrative into which he step...
australia.content:
Along the main drag of Noosa Heads, expensive beachfront villas and resorts meld into designer-boho apparel stores, upmarket restaurants and bars and pizza joints. Kids with sandy feet and hair still dripping from the surf slurp gelati alongside activewear-clad women who have descended from the scrubby headland.

The beachside town is a holiday destination for middle-class families as well as the wealthy, and is a particular favourite with Victorians. And those who headed there for the recent King’s birthday long weekend were treated to plenty of Queensland sun.

But on Sunday, Queensland police alleged something darker had occurred that weekend on Hastings Street. They charged a 46-year-old Victorian man with assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting. The man was refused bail. The victim or victims were not identified, in line with Queensland laws, neither was the person who called the police.

Before he had even faced court, word had leaked that the accused man was very high profile. Media began naming him as the fitness influencer Sam Wood. He had come to public attention in 2015 as a contestant on the dating show, The Bachelor, then at the peak of its popularity in Australia, and married the woman he met there, Snezana Markoski, with whom he built both a family and a series of fitness and wellness enterprises.

On Monday, Wood’s lawyer told media that the star intended to “defend the charges”.

A statement posted to social media accounts of the husband and wife said: “This is a difficult time for all of us, we are working through this as a family and are thoroughly co-operating with authorities.”

On Thursday he was denied bail. The Maroochydore magistrates court heard Snezana, who was allegedly choked and assaulted by Wood, told police she “thought she was going to die”.

The cultural prominence of Wood, his sustained commercial success, and the sudden, thunderous collapse of his empire this week, was shaped to a great extent more than a decade ago, by the confected TV narrative into which he first stepped.

Reality TV in the mid 2010s was at the crest of its second wave. The Bachelor Australia, launched many years after its US parent, never quite managed the ratings heights of its competitors, and the show’s saccharine romance and engineered drama felt anachronistic and regressive. It nevertheless grew in popularity over its first two seasons, with an ecosystem of live-tweeters and recapping bloggers feeding on the minutiae of every episode, often with knowing cynicism. Indeed, for many – if not most – of its viewers, the irony was part of the appeal.

At the end of the second season, the drama had spilled outside the show’s heavily manipulated narrative: more than a million viewers had watched Bachelor Blake Garvey propose marriage to then-marketing assistant Sam Frost, only for the network to issue a statement the following morning explaining the couple had already split up. Garvey was soon revealed to be dating the show’s runner-up. Irony notwithstanding, consumers of romance hate seeing the heroine get jilted. There was increasing pressure to ensure the third Bachelor was a verifiable good guy.

Enter Wood, 34, a Tasmanian-born Melbourne-based personal trainer. He reportedly applied for season three having never watched an episode of the show, after a client at his Brighton-based gym, the Woodshed, insisted. Over the course of 16 episodes he lumbered along on cut-budget “dates”, whittling down his potential matches one by one, until he finally handed his last rose, the show’s love token, to 34-year-old Perth-based Snezana Markoski.

Snezana claimed she had been convinced to go on the show by her then-eight-year-old daughter, Eve. Her status as a single mother was an early plot point, edited throughout to suggest her “winning” Sam was an outside chance. Thus she became the unlikely heroine who stole the heart of the TV hero. The couple’s post-show relationship also appeared to defy cynicism about its origins: Snezana moved to Melbourne, Wood proposed, the couple got married and had three more children.

Meanwhile, they leveraged Wood’s increased profile, particularly among women, into significantly lucrative commercial ventures. At the time of his performance on the Bachelor, Wood was the owner of GeckoSports, a kids’ fitness franchise network. He sold it in 2016 to startup online fitness and health program 28 by Sam Wood, which grew rapidly, ballooning during Covid lockdowns and claiming more than 400,000 subscribers over its first six years.

The hyperreal television romance also morphed seamlessly into a shiny Instagram presence, replete with happy-family snaps and sponcon galore. Companies that have had commercial partnerships with Wood since his Bachelor appearance are numerous, including Weet-Bix, Mercedes-Benz, Under Armour, 2XU, Australian Eggs, MYOB, Vibe Soda, Remedy Drinks, and health insurer Bupa. (Many are now making clear those partnerships are long over.) He was a regular face on morning television, and lifestyle shows like Better Homes and Gardens.

In 2022, Wood sold 28 to myDNA, a Melbourne genomics company backed by pharmaceuticals mogul Dennis Bastas, for $71.2m, a 5% stake in the parent company, and an agreement that he would remain the face of the program.

Wood built his post-Bachelor empire off his family-friendly, women-friendly image. He sustained it by appearing to be the robust exception that proved the rule about “nice guys” on reality TV. The first major dent was Ollo for Women: his attempt earlier this year to couple his core product, fitness and meal planning, with telehealth consults and GLP-1 assisted weight loss. Some saw it as a betrayal of his principles, though Wood did not agree.

But his public image was always contradictory. He was the tanned and muscular leading man with the toothpaste-ad smile, who nevertheless remained down to earth, plain-speaking and polite. He was the rich and dashing romance hero, and yet the committed family man, father of daughters. He was, as a glowing 2023 profile in Men’s Health put it, the “de facto embodiment of Australian masculinity”.

On Monday, as news about the domestic violence allegations gathered steam, businesses and other fitness influencers began distancing themselves from Wood, in some cases breaking off active commercial agreements. Ollo’s social media accounts were deactivated. DBG Health, the ultimate owners of 28, put Wood on indefinite leave, and changed the cover image on the fitness program’s Facebook page from a smiling group shot of Wood, Snezana and other personal trainers, to a generic picture of a smartphone app.

On Tuesday, the company Wood had built “ended its commercial relationships with Sam Wood, effective immediately”. “DBG Health does not tolerate domestic violence in any form, and our thoughts are with anyone affected by it,” a spokesperson said, noting 28 would continue under the leadership of Mark Watkin, previously its chief operating officer.

“I was a pretty quiet, self-conscious kid from Tassie,” Wood said in that 2023 profile.

“Even now I have moments of impostor syndrome and disbelief that this whole thing has reached the levels that it has, almost like I don’t belong here and the whole thing could come crashing down at any moment.”

Wood returns to court on 23 November.

  • Support for anyone affected by the subject matter of this report is available at Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578)

australia.title: Queensland literary awards: ‘stunning’ debut inspired by segregated shantytown wins top prize
australia.snippet: Lenora Thaker wins $30,000 prize for ‘a work of state significance’ for The Pearl of Tagai Town, which draws on her family’s history in C...
australia.content:
A “stunning” debut novel described as “unambiguously and distinctively Queensland” has won the $30,000 top prize at the Queensland literary awards (QLAs).

Meriam and Wagedagam author Lenora Thaker won the Queensland premier’s award for a work of state significance for her historical novel The Pearl of Tagai Town, which was inspired by her ancestors’ lives in an unmapped shantytown known as Cairns-Malay Town. The town once housed Indigenous Australians, Chinese, Indian, Japanese, Malaysian and Sri Lankan residents who had been segregated from the white population; it existed from the late 1800s until the late 1950s.

The QLA judges praised Thaker’s “accessible and deeply enjoyable” book for its “vivid sense of place”.

“Warm, richly drawn characters and an innovative integration of Ailan languages come together in a rich, cohesive whole, bringing new insight and fresh imaginative life to a far north Queensland community. The Pearl of Tagai Town is a stunning debut novel,” the judges wrote in a joint statement.

The winners were announced at a ceremony on Thursday night at Brisbane Powerhouse, as part of Brisbane writers festival.

Claire Thomas won the $15,000 fiction category for On Not Climbing Mountains, which follows a woman on a trip in Switzerland, who distracts herself from grief with research on famous names who had connections to the country.

The $15,000 nonfiction prize went to Find Me at the Jaffa Gate: An Encyclopaedia of a Palestinian Family by Australian-Palestinian writer Micaela Sahhar, about how her family’s story was shaped by the Nakba, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel during the country’s founding in 1948. Sahhar won the same category at the Victorian premier’s literary awards in February.

The $15,000 children’s book category was won by Once I Was a Giant by Zeno Sworder, which has also won book of the year at the Australian Book Industry awards and the children’s category at the Victorian premier’s literary award. Illustrated and written by Sworder, the book tells the tale of a tree transformed into a pencil that then writes its own story.

Julianne Negri won the $15,000 young adult category for her book The Belly of a Wolf, Helena Pantsis won the $15,000 short story category for her collection Mother Salad, and Eunice Andrada won the $17,500 poetry category for her collection Kontra.

The $15,000 people’s choice category was won by Sita Walker’s debut In a Common Hour, a novel that takes place across a single hour at a state high school. Walker has been a teacher for more than 20 years, and currently teaches English at a high school in Brisbane’s south-east.

Founded in 1999, the QLAs were previously known as the Queensland premier’s literary awards until 2012, when they were abolished by then premier Campbell Newman. Queensland’s literary community intervened to keep the awards alive.

The QLAs were administered by the State Library of Queensland from 2014 until 2025, when the awards were embroiled in controversy over the arts minister John-Paul Langbroek’s intervention to stop the library awarding a $15,000 fellowship to First Nations author K A Ren Wyld, over a social media post about the dead Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar.

Wyld said she had posted the comment in an “emotional moment”, and that her winning manuscript had nothing to do with Gaza.

Twelve QLA judges resigned in protest of Wyld’s treatment, leading to last year’s awards being delayed. Langbroek eventually handed their management over to the Brisbane writers festival from this year.

2026 Queensland literary awards: winners list

Queensland premier’s award for a work of state significance: The Pearl of Tagai Town by Lenora Thaker

Steele Rudd award for a short story collection: Mother Salad by Helena Pantsis

Judith Wright Calanthe award for a poetry collection: KONTRA by Eunice Andrada

Children’s book award: Once I Was a Giant by Zeno Sworder

Young adult book award: The Belly of a Wolf by Julianne Negri

Fiction book award: On Not Climbing Mountains by Claire Thomas

Nonfiction book award: Find Me at the Jaffa Gate by Micaela Sahhar

Lord mayor’s people’s choice Queensland book of the year award: In a Common Hour by Sita Walker

world.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province
world.snippet: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebo...
world.content:
Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.

This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.

A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.

The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.

Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.

He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).

Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.

He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.

Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.

Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.

After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.

The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.

The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.

“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”

The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.

Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”

North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

world.title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads
world.snippet: Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again As renewed fighting has thr...
world.content:
As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.

Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.

The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.

Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.

The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.

Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.

Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.

“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.

“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”

In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.

Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.

“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”

Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.

“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.

The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.

Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”

Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.

Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.

An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.

* Names have been changed to protect their identities

world.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
world.snippet: After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underw...
world.content:
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.

Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.

After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.

Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.

“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.

“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”

On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.

“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”

Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.

When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”

The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.

In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.

“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”

With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.

She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.

“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

world.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
world.snippet: Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory Court officials and craftspeopl...
world.content:
Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.

The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.

Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”

The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.

But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.

Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.

“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century,” Campbell told the Guardian, but she said this was the first study to look at trauma and cause of death while examining human remains from the tombs.

Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.

Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.

The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.

“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”

Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.

Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.

She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”

Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.

“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

world.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
world.snippet: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown An Egyptian journalist has...
world.content:
An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.

Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.

On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.

Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.

Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.

“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”

The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.

Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.

The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.

More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.

The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.

The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.

This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.

While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”

Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.

Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.

Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.
